title: Why typing in a huge file doesn't lag

post.caption: Your editor never stores your file as one big string. It uses a rope: a tree of small chunks that makes every edit cost the same, anywhere in the file.

scenes.title: Type into a *100 MB* file. ==No lag.==
scenes.narration: Type one letter into a 100 MB file, and your editor doesn't lag. Here's the trick.

scenes.heading: One long string
scenes.note: Insert near the top of a big file and almost all of it moves.
scenes.narration: If your file were one long string, every insert means shifting every byte after the cursor, one by one.

scenes.label: copied for *one* letter
scenes.narration: That's up to a hundred megabytes copied, for a single letter.

scenes.heading: A rope: a *tree* of small strings

highlight.note: Skip 11 on the left, land in one chunk

scenes.narration: Editors use a rope instead. It's a balanced tree. Each branch counts the characters below it, and the leaves hold small chunks of text. To find character fifteen, walk down: skip the left eleven, and land in one small chunk.

nodes.label: Walk down to the leaf
nodes.sub: a few hops, even for huge files

nodes.label: Edit one small chunk
nodes.sub: a few hundred bytes at most

nodes.label: Update counts on the way up

scenes.narration: Inserting is three steps. Walk down to the right leaf. Edit that one small chunk. Then update the counts on the way back up.

scenes.heading: Bytes touched in a *100 MB* file
scenes.narration: Compare the work. A plain string moves up to a hundred million bytes. A rope touches about a thousand.
In Rust, the ropey crate gives you this for free. Insert anywhere in logarithmic time, and look up any line just as fast.

scenes.heading: Three wins for *free*
items: Undo is cheap: versions share chunks
Line numbers are tracked for you
scenes.narration: So ropes give you three things. Edits cost the same anywhere in the file. Undo is cheap, because old versions share chunks. And line numbers come for free.

scenes.title: Small chunks. ==Big files.==
scenes.narration: Small chunks, big files. Follow for more editor internals.
